div.p: Whether it were the harder thing or the greater, Brutus, to refuse you when you ask the same favour again and again, or to accomplish what you ask, I have long and often debated. For to refuse one whom I love beyond all others, and by whom I feel that I am held most dear—especially when his request is just and his desire honourable—seemed to me decidedly harsh; yet to undertake a task so great that it is difficult not only to carry out by skill but even to grasp in thought, I judged scarcely to belong to a man who shrinks from the censure of the learned and the discerning.

For what is greater than this: that, when there is so wide a difference among good orators, one should judge which is the best kind and, so to speak, the very form of speaking? And since you ask me this so often, I will set my hand to it, not so much in the hope of carrying it through as out of a willingness to make the attempt; for I would rather, having complied with your zeal, that you should miss my discernment than, if I had not done so, my goodwill.

You ask, then, and now for the more often, which kind of eloquence I most approve, and what that thing seems to me to be to which nothing can be added, which I judge supreme and most perfect. In this I fear that, if I achieve what you wish and portray the orator you seek, I may slacken the zeal of many who, broken by despair, will be unwilling to attempt what they distrust their power to attain.

But it is fitting that all should attempt all things, who have set their hearts on great things and on things to be sought with great effort. And if any man either falls short by nature in that force of surpassing genius, or is less well equipped with the discipline of the great arts, let him nonetheless hold to the course he can; for in following first place it is honourable to come to rest in the second or the third. For among the poets—to speak of the Greeks—there is room not for Homer alone, or Archilochus or Sophocles or Pindar, but for those who stand second to these, or even below the second.

Nor indeed did the greatness of Plato deter Aristotle from writing in philosophy, nor did Aristotle himself, by his admirable learning and abundance, quench the studies of the rest. And not only were excellent men not deterred from the noblest pursuits, but not even the craftsmen withdrew from their arts, who could not match the beauty of the Ialysus, which we saw at Rhodes, or of the Coan Venus; nor, deterred by the image of Olympian Jupiter or the statue of the Spear-bearer, did the rest make less trial of what they could accomplish, or how far they might advance; and of these so great was the multitude, so great in each one's own kind was the praise, that, while we marvelled at the highest, we yet approved the lower.

Among orators, however—the Greek ones at least—it is wonderful how far one man surpasses all the rest; and yet, when there was a Demosthenes, there were many great and famous orators, and there had been before, nor were any lacking afterward. For which reason there is no cause why the hope of those who have given themselves to the study of eloquence should be broken, or their industry grow faint; for neither is that very thing which is best to be despaired of, and in surpassing things those are great which come nearest to the best.

And for my part, in fashioning the supreme orator, I shall shape him such as perhaps no one ever was. For I do not ask who he was, but what that thing is than which nothing could be more excellent—a thing which in the unbroken sweep of speaking does not often, and I am inclined to think never, shine forth, but which in some part may at times shine, more densely in some, more rarely perhaps in others.

But this is my settled view: that there is nothing in any kind so beautiful but that there is something more beautiful from which it is, as it were, an image expressed from some original face; and this cannot be perceived by the eyes or the ears or by any sense, but we grasp it by thought and mind alone. And so, in the case both of the statues of Phidias, than which we see nothing in that kind more perfect, and of those paintings I have named, we can yet conceive of things more beautiful; nor indeed did that artist, when he made the form of Jupiter or of Minerva,

contemplate any one from whom he might draw the likeness; rather, in his own mind there dwelt a certain surpassing form of beauty, and gazing upon it and fixed upon it he directed his art and his hand toward its likeness. As, therefore, in forms and figures there is something perfect and excellent, by imitation of whose conceived form the works of art are referred and which itself falls under the eyes, so we behold with the mind the form of perfect eloquence, while we seek with the ears its likeness.

These forms of things Plato calls Ideas—that gravest authority and master not only of understanding but of speaking; and he denies that they come to be, and says that they exist forever and are contained by reason and intelligence; all else is born, perishes, flows, slips away, and does not remain longer in one and the same state. Whatever, then, there is concerning which we reason by method and rule, that is to be brought back to the ultimate form and aspect of its own kind.

And I see that this first step of mine is drawn not from the disputations of the rhetoricians but fetched from the heart of philosophy, and that, being at once ancient and somewhat obscure, it will meet with either some censure or at least some wonder. For men will either marvel what these things have to do with the matters we seek—and for them the case itself, once understood, will give satisfaction, so that it may seem to have been fetched from afar not without reason—or they will censure us because we explore untrodden paths and leave the beaten ones.

But I, for my part, both am aware that I often seem to say new things, when I am saying things very old but unheard by most, and I confess that I—orator, if indeed I am one, or whatever sort I am—came forth not from the workshops of the rhetoricians but from the walks of the Academy; for those are the courses of manifold and varied discourses, in which the footprints of Plato were first impressed. But by his disputations and those of the other philosophers the orator has been both most stirred and most aided; for all the richness and, as it were, the woodland of speech is drawn from them, and yet not sufficiently equipped for forensic cases, which, as they themselves were wont to say, they left to the ruder Muses.

Thus this forensic eloquence, scorned and rejected by the philosophers, lacked indeed many great aids; yet, adorned with words and thoughts, it won applause among the people and did not greatly fear the judgment and censure of the few: so that to the learned there was wanting popular eloquence, and to the eloquent elegant learning.

Let it then be laid down first—what will afterward be the better understood—that without philosophy the man we seek cannot be made eloquent; not, however, that everything is in it, but that it helps as the wrestling-school helps the actor; for small things are often most rightly compared with great. For no one can speak more broadly and abundantly of great and varied matters without philosophy;—

seeing that even in Plato's Phaedrus Socrates says that Pericles surpassed the other orators in this, that he had been a hearer of the natural philosopher Anaxagoras; from whom he reckons that, along with certain other splendid and lofty things, he learned this too, that he became rich and fruitful, and knew—which is the greatest thing in eloquence—by what modes of speech each part of men's minds is stirred; the same may be thought of Demosthenes, from whose letters

it may be understood how frequent a hearer he was of Plato;—nor indeed without the discipline of the philosophers can we discern the genus and species of each thing, nor unfold it by definition, nor distribute it into its parts, nor judge what is true and what false, nor discern what is consequent, see what is contradictory, distinguish what is ambiguous. What shall I say of the nature of things, the knowledge of which supplies great abundance to speech; of life, of duties, of virtue, of character? Can these be either spoken of or understood at all without much discipline in those very matters?

To these so many and so great matters there must be applied innumerable adornments; which alone, indeed, were at that time handed down by those who were reckoned masters of speaking; whence it comes about that no one attains that true and finished eloquence, because the discipline of understanding is one thing and that of speaking another, and the knowledge of matters is sought from some teachers, that of words from others.

And so Marcus Antonius, to whom the age of our fathers assigned almost the first place in eloquence—a man by nature exceedingly keen and discerning—in that one book which he left behind says that he had seen many men eloquent of speech, but no one eloquent in the full sense. Plainly there dwelt in his mind a form of eloquence which he discerned with his mind but did not see in actual fact. And being a man of the keenest genius—for so he was—he, desiring much both in himself and in others, saw no one who could rightly be called eloquent; and if he thought neither himself nor Lucius Crassus eloquent,

he surely held in his mind some comprehended form of eloquence, to which, since nothing was wanting, he could not admit within that form those who lacked one thing or several. Let us track down this man, then, Brutus, if we can—the man whom Antonius never saw, or who never existed at all; and if we cannot imitate and express him—which that same Antonius said had scarcely been granted to a god—we may perhaps be able to say what sort of man he ought to be.

There are in all three kinds of speaking, in each one of which certain men have flourished, but in all of them, which is what we want, very few have flourished equally. For there have been the grand-speaking, so to call them, with ample and weighty thoughts and majesty of words—vehement, varied, copious, weighty, equipped and ready to move and turn men's minds; and this very thing some achieved with a rough, harsh, bristling style, not rounded and brought to a close, others with one smooth, well-built, and shapely. And on the other side there have been the plain, the keen, who teach everything and make it clearer rather than fuller, polished with a certain subtle and compressed style; and within that same kind some are shrewd but unpolished and deliberately like the rude and the unskilled, others within the same leanness are neater, that is to say witty, even flowering and lightly adorned.

There is, moreover, a certain middle kind set between these and, as it were, tempered, using neither the keen edge of the latter nor the thunderbolt of the former, neighbour to both, excelling in neither, partaking of each—or rather, if we seek the truth, lacking each; and it flows in one even tenor, as they say, in speaking, bringing nothing but ease and evenness, or it adds a few clusters, as it were, in a garland, and distinguishes the whole speech with modest adornments of words and thoughts.

Whoever have attained the power of these several kinds, each in its own, have had a great name among orators. But the question must be asked whether they have achieved what we want. For we see that there have been some who could speak the same matters both ornately and weightily, and the same shrewdly and plainly. And would that among the Latins we could find the likeness of such an orator! It would be an excellent thing not to seek the foreign, but to be content with what is our own.

But I—the same who, in that discourse of ours set out in the Brutus, granted much to the Latins, whether to encourage others or because I loved my own people—I remember that I set one man, Demosthenes, far before all; and him I would adjust to the eloquence I conceive in my mind, not to that which I myself have known in some particular person. None has appeared more weighty than he, none more shrewd, none more tempered. And so we must admonish those whose unskilled talk has grown common, who either desire to be called Attic or themselves wish to speak in the Attic manner, that they should most of all admire this man, in comparison with whom I do not believe that even Athens itself was more Attic; let them learn what the Attic is, and let them measure his eloquence by its own powers, not by their own weakness.

For now each man praises only so much as he hopes he can imitate. But still I think it not amiss to teach those endowed with the best zeal but a less firm judgment what is the proper praise of the Attic writers. The discernment of the hearers has always been the governess of the orators' eloquence. For all who wish to win approval look to the will of those who hear, and to it, and to their judgment and nod, they wholly fashion and fit themselves.

And so Caria and Phrygia and Mysia, because they are the least polished and least elegant, took up, as suited to their ears, a certain rich and, as it were, fattened kind of diction, which their neighbours the Rhodians—with no very wide sea between—never approved, and which the Athenians utterly rejected; whose judgment was always discerning and pure, so that they could endure to hear nothing but what was uncorrupted and elegant. While the orator served their scruple, he dared to set down no insolent word, none offensive.

And so this man, whom we have said surpassed the rest, in that oration for Ctesiphon—by far his best—spoke from the outset more subdued, then, while he disputes about the laws, more compressed; afterward, kindling the judges by degrees, when he saw them aflame, in what remained he exulted more boldly. And yet, in this very speaker who weighs carefully the weight of all his words, Aeschines censures certain things and assails them, and mocking calls them harsh, offensive, intolerable; nay, he even asks of him—when indeed he calls him a beast—whether those are words or monstrous prodigies; so that to Aeschines not even Demosthenes seems to speak in the Attic manner.

For it is easy to mark some burning word, so to speak, and, when the fires of the mind are now quenched, to laugh at it. And so Demosthenes, clearing himself, makes a jest: he denies that the fortunes of Greece rested on this—whether he used this word or that, whether he stretched out his hand to this side or to that. In what manner, then, would a Mysian or a Phrygian be heard at Athens, when even Demosthenes is assailed as turgid? But when, with bent and howling voice, in the Asiatic manner, a man had begun to sing, who would endure him, or rather who would not order him to be carried off?

To the Attic ears, therefore, polished and scrupulous, those who fit themselves are to be reckoned as speaking in the Attic manner. Of these there are many kinds; these men, however, suspect of only one kind what it is. For they think that whoever speaks roughly and uncouthly—provided he do it elegantly and cleanly—he alone speaks in the Attic manner. They err in saying "alone"; in saying "Attic," they are not deceived.

For by their judgment, if that alone is Attic, not even Pericles spoke in the Attic manner, to whom the first place was without dispute assigned; who, if he had used the plain kind, would never have been said by the poet Aristophanes to flash and thunder and to confound Greece. Let that most charming and most polished writer Lysias, then, speak in the Attic manner—for who could deny it?—provided we understand this to be Attic in Lysias, not that he is plain and unadorned, but that he has nothing insolent or inept; whereas to speak ornately and weightily and copiously must be either the property of the Attic writers, or else neither Aeschines nor Demosthenes is Attic.

But see, some men profess themselves Thucydideans: a strange new and unheard-of breed of the unskilled. For those who follow Lysias follow a certain advocate—not, indeed, an ample and grand one, yet subtle and elegant and one who could take his stand splendidly in forensic cases. Thucydides, however, narrates deeds done and wars and battles, weightily indeed and well, but nothing can be transferred from him to forensic and public use. Those very harangues have so many obscure and hidden thoughts that they can scarcely be understood; which in civil oratory is the very greatest of faults.

But what is this great perversity in men, that, with corn discovered, they should feed on acorns? Could the diet of men have been refined by the kindness of the Athenians, but their speech could not? Who, moreover, of the Greek rhetoricians ever drew anything from Thucydides? "But he was praised by all." I grant it; yet only as a prudent, severe, and weighty unfolder of events—not as one who handled cases in the courts, but as one who narrated wars in his histories; and so he was never reckoned an orator.

Nor indeed, had he not written history, would his name survive, especially since he had been a man of honour and noble birth. Yet no one imitates the weight either of his words or of his thoughts; but when men have spoken certain maimed and gaping phrases, which they could have made even without a master, they think themselves true-born Thucydideans. I have even met with one who desired to be like Xenophon, whose speech is indeed sweeter than honey, but most remote from the din of the forum.

Let us turn back, then, to him whom we wish to begin upon, and to be fashioned at last with that eloquence which Antonius found in no man. A great and arduous work, in truth, Brutus, we undertake; but nothing is hard, I think, to one who loves. And I love, and have always loved, your genius, your studies, your character. Moreover, I am kindled more each day, not by longing alone—by which indeed I am consumed, missing our meetings, the familiarity of our daily life, your most learned conversations—but also by the incredible fame of your admirable virtues, which, though unlike in appearance, are joined by your discernment.

For what is so far apart as affability from severity? Yet who was ever held either more upright than you, or more agreeable? What is so difficult as, in deciding the disputes of very many, to be loved by all? Yet you bring it about that you send away even those against whom you decide both fair-minded and appeased. And so you achieve this, that though you do nothing for the sake of winning favour, yet all that you do is welcome. Therefore of all lands Gaul alone does not burn in the common conflagration; in which you enjoy your own self, since you are known to be present in the light of Italy and move among the flower or the strength of the best citizens. And how great is this, that amid the greatest occupations you never intermit the pursuits of learning, but always either yourself write something or call me to writing!

And so I set my hand to this work straightway after the Cato was finished—which I should never have touched, fearing the times that are hostile to virtue, had I not deemed it a wrong not to obey you, who urged me and stirred up the memory, dear to me, of that man—but I call you to witness that, asked by you, and reluctant, I have dared to write these things. For I wish the charge to be shared with you, so that, if I should not be able to sustain so great an inquiry, the blame for the unjust burden laid upon me may be yours, the blame for accepting it mine; in which, however, the error of our judgment will be made good by the praise of the office assigned by you.

But in every matter the most difficult thing is to set forth the form of the best—what is called in Greek the character—because what is best seems different to different men. "I delight in Ennius," says one, "because he does not depart from the common usage of words"; "I in Pacuvius," says another: with this man all the verses are adorned and elaborated, with the former far more carelessly; make a third prefer Accius. For judgments are various, as among the Greeks, nor is it easy to unfold what form most excels. In paintings some are delighted by the rough, the uncouth, the hidden, and the shadowy, others, on the contrary, by the bright, the cheerful, the well-lit. What is there by which you might express some rule or formula, when each thing excels in its own kind, and the kinds are many? By this scruple I have not been driven back from this attempt; and I have reckoned that in all things there is something best, even if it lie hidden, and that it can be judged by one who is skilled in that matter.

But since there are several kinds of orations, and these diverse, nor do they all fall into one form—those of panegyrics and histories and such persuasive pieces as Isocrates made his Panegyricus, and many others who are named sophists, and the form of the rest of those writings which stand apart from forensic contention and from that whole kind which in Greek is called epideictic, because it is prepared, as it were, for inspection for the sake of delight—I shall not embrace these at this time; not that they are to be neglected, for that is, as it were, the nurse of the orator whom we wish to fashion and concerning whom we are striving to say something more exquisite. By it both the abundance of words is nourished, and their arrangement and rhythm enjoy a certain freer licence.

Pardon, too, is granted to the trimness of thoughts, and the witty, sure, and circumscribed roundings of words are allowed; and deliberately—not by ambush, but openly and in the open—it is wrought, so that word answers to word as if measured out and matched, so that opposites are often set side by side and contraries compared, and so that the ends are alike terminated and return the same sound in their falling; which things, in the reality of cases, we both do far more rarely and certainly more covertly. In the Panathenaicus, indeed, Isocrates confesses that he pursued these things zealously; for he had written not for the contest of the courts, but for the pleasure of the ears.

These devices, they say, Thrasymachus of Chalcedon first handled, and Gorgias of Leontini, then Theodorus of Byzantium and many others, whom Socrates in the Phaedrus calls "word-craftsmen"; of whose work much is clever enough, but, like things newly and just now coming to birth, minute and resembling little verses and overmuch painted. Wherefore the more wonderful are Herodotus and Thucydides; whose age, though it fell within the times of those I have named, were nonetheless themselves furthest removed from such dainties—or rather follies. For the one flows on without any roughness, like a calm river; the other is borne along more impetuously and, on warlike matters, sings even in a kind of war-note; and by these first, as Theophrastus says, history was set in motion, so that it dared to speak more richly and more ornately than its predecessors.

To the age of these succeeded Isocrates, who beyond all others of the same kind is always praised by us, though sometimes, Brutus, with your gentle and learned resistance; but you will perhaps grant me my point, if you come to know what I praise in him. For when Thrasymachus seemed to him chopped up by minute rhythms, and Gorgias too—who yet are handed down as the first to have joined words by a certain art—and Theodorus, on the other hand, too abrupt and not, so to speak, sufficiently rounded, he was the first to set about expanding sentences with words and filling them out with softer rhythms; and in this, since he taught those who became leaders, some in speaking, some in writing, his house was held to be the workshop of eloquence.

And so, as I, when I was being praised by our Cato, easily endured to be blamed by the rest, so Isocrates seems, on the testimony of Plato, to be able to despise the judgments of others. For there is, as you know, on, as it were, the last page of the Phaedrus, Socrates speaking in these very words: "Still a young man even now, Phaedrus, is Isocrates, but I am willing to say what I prophesy of him." "What, pray?" says the other. "He seems to me to be of greater genius than to be compared with the speeches of Lysias, and besides, of a greater bent toward virtue; so that it will be no wonder at all if, when he has advanced in age, he either, in this kind of speeches to which he now devotes himself, so far surpasses all the other boys who have ever touched oratory as a man surpasses children, or, if he is not content with these, by some divine impulse of mind he aspires to greater things; for there is by nature a certain philosophy in this man's mind."

These things Socrates prophesies of the young man. But these things of the older man Plato writes—and he writes as his contemporary; and he, the assailer of all the rhetoricians, admires this one alone; and as for me, let those who do not love Isocrates suffer me to err together with Socrates and Plato. A sweet kind of oratory, then, and free and flowing, witty in its thoughts, sonorous in its words, is found in that epideictic kind which we have said is the property of the sophists—fitter for show than for battle, dedicated to the gymnasium and the wrestling-school, scorned and driven from the forum. But since eloquence itself, reared on these nourishments, afterward colours and strengthens itself, it was not amiss to speak of the orator's cradle, as it were. But these things belong to games and pageantry; let us now come into the battle-line and the combat.

Since there are three things the orator must look to—what he says, and in what place each thing, and in what manner—we must indeed say what is best in each, but in a manner somewhat other than is usual in the handing-down of an art. We shall set down no precepts, for that we have not undertaken, but we shall sketch the appearance and form of excellent eloquence; nor shall we set forth by what means it is acquired, but what sort of thing it seems to us to be.

And first, two things briefly; for they are not so much marks of the highest praise as necessary, and yet almost common to many men. For both to find and to judge what one is to say are indeed great things, and, as it were, the soul within the body, but they belong more to discernment than to eloquence: and yet in what case is discernment idle? Let this orator, then, whom we wish to be supreme, know the topics of arguments and reasonings.

For since, whatever it is that turns on controversy or on contention, in it the question is either whether a thing is, or what it is, or of what quality it is:—whether it is, by signs; what it is, by definitions; of what quality it is, by the parts of right and wrong; that the orator may be able to use these—not the common orator, but this excellent one—let him always, if he can, draw the controversy away from particular persons and times; for one may dispute more broadly about the genus than about the part, so that what has been proved in the universal must of necessity be proved in the part;—

this question, then, drawn from particular persons and times to the principle of the universal kind, is called thesis. In this Aristotle trained the young, not in the manner of the philosophers, to dispute subtly, but for the abundance of the rhetoricians, on both sides, that a thing might be said the more ornately and richly; and he handed down the topics—for so he calls them—as it were the marks of arguments, from which a speech might be drawn on either side.

This man of ours, then—for we seek not some declaimer from the school or a brawler from the forum, but the most learned and most perfect of men—will, since fixed topics are handed down, run through them all, use the apt ones, speak generically; whence flow also those that are called commonplaces. Nor indeed will he use this abundance without discernment, but will weigh and select all things; for not always nor in all cases do arguments of the same weight come from the same topics.

He will therefore bring judgment to bear, and will not only find what to say but will also weigh it. For nothing is more fruitful than men's minds, especially those that are cultivated by disciplines. But as fertile and rich cornfields pour forth not only the crops but also weeds most hostile to the crops, so sometimes from those topics there are born certain things either trivial, or foreign to the cases, or useless. And unless great selection of these is brought to bear by the orator's judgment,

in what manner will he cling and dwell among his own good points, or soften the hard ones, or hide what cannot be dissolved and altogether crush them, if he may, or turn aside men's minds, or bring forward something else which, set against the obstacle, may be more plausible than that which stands in the way?

And now with what diligence will he arrange the things he has found? Since that was the second of the three. He will doubtless make honourable porches and illustrious approaches to the case; and when he has seized men's minds at the first onset, he will weaken and shut out what is against him; of his strongest points he will set some first, some last, and will press the lighter ones home in between.

And in the first two parts of speaking we have described summarily and briefly what sort of man he ought to be. But, as was said before, in these parts, though they are weighty and great, there is less both of art and of labour; whereas, when he has found both what and in what place he is to say it, that is by far the greatest thing—to see in what manner. For it is well said—what our Carneades was wont to say—that Clitomachus said the same things, but Charmadas said them in the same manner too. And if in philosophy it matters so much in what manner you speak, where the matter is regarded and the words are not weighed, what, pray, is to be thought in cases which the speech wholly governs?

And this indeed, Brutus, I perceived from your letters—that you were not inquiring this, what sort of orator I would have to be supreme in finding and in arranging, but you seemed to me to ask this: what kind of the actual oratory itself I judged best—a difficult thing, immortal gods, and of all things the most difficult. For since oratory is supple and tender, and so flexible that it follows wherever you turn it, then varied natures and inclinations have produced kinds of speaking widely differing among themselves:

a flood of words and volubility are dear to some, who place eloquence in the speed of utterance; distinct and pointed intervals, pauses and breathings-out delight others: what can be so diverse? Yet in both there is something excellent. Some labour at smoothness and evenness and a pure and, as it were, candid kind of speaking; behold, others pursue a certain hardness and severity in their words and a kind of sadness in their oratory; and—what we divided a little before, that some wish to seem weighty, some plain, some tempered—as many kinds of orations as we have said there are, just so many kinds of orators are found.

And since I have now begun to swell this office more fully than was asked of you—for to you, asking only about the kind of oratory, I have answered briefly even about finding and arranging—I shall now not speak about the manner of oratory alone, but also about delivery: so that no part will be passed over, since indeed concerning memory nothing need be said in this place, which is common to many arts.

But in what manner a thing is delivered consists in two things, in action and in utterance. For action is, as it were, a certain eloquence of the body, since it consists of voice and movement. The changes of the voice are as many as those of the minds, which are most of all moved by the voice. And so that perfect orator, whom our discourse has long been pointing to, in whatever way he wishes to seem affected himself and the mind of the hearer to be moved, will bring to bear an appropriate tone of voice; concerning which I would say more, if this were a time for precepts or if you were asking this. I would speak also of gesture, with which the countenance is joined; in all of which it can scarcely be said how much it matters in what manner the orator uses them.

For the inarticulate have often borne off the fruit of eloquence by the dignity of their action, and many of the eloquent have been thought inarticulate through the unsightliness of their delivery; so that not without cause did Demosthenes assign to delivery the first place, and the second, and the third; for if there is no eloquence without it, while it itself, without eloquence, is so great, surely it can do most in speaking. He, then, who seeks the chief place in eloquence will wish both to speak fiercely with a strained voice, and gently with a subdued one, and to seem weighty with a lowered voice, and pitiful with a bent one;

for there is a certain wonderful nature in the voice, of which—of its three tones in all, the bent, the high, and the low—so great and so sweet a variety is perfected in song. There is, moreover, even in speaking a certain more hidden song—not this peroration of the rhetoricians of Phrygia and Caria, almost a chant, but that which Demosthenes and Aeschines mean, when the one casts in the other's teeth his inflections of voice; for Demosthenes even says that the man whom he often mentions used to wail with a sweet and clear voice.

In which this too seems to me worth noting, toward the pursuit of sweetness in the voice: for Nature herself, as if she were tuning the speech of men, placed in every word a high tone, and not more than one, nor further from the last syllable than the third; the more, therefore, should industry follow Nature as its guide to the pleasure of the ears.

And goodness of voice indeed is to be wished for; for it is not in our power, but the management and use of it are in our power. Therefore that prince of orators will vary and change it: pursuing all the degrees of tones, now straining, now relaxing them. And likewise he will so use movement that nothing is in excess. In gesture the carriage upright and lofty; pacing seldom and not far; advance moderate and that too rare; no softness of the neck, no nimble play of the fingers, no joint falling to a measured beat; governing himself rather by the whole trunk and by a manly bending of the sides, by a thrusting out of the arm in vehement passages, by a drawing in of it in the calmer ones.

But the countenance, which after the voice has the most power—how much dignity and how much charm will it bring! In which, when you have brought it about that there be nothing inept or grimacing, then there is need of a certain great control of the eyes. For as the countenance is the image of the mind, so the eyes are its tokens; and the measure both of their gladness and, in turn, of their sadness the very matters under discussion will temper.

But now the appearance of that perfect orator and of the highest eloquence must be expressed. That he excels in this one thing, while all else lies hidden in him, the very name indicates; for he who has embraced all these things is called neither "inventor" nor "composer" nor "actor," but in Greek, from "to speak," rhetor, and in Latin "eloquent"; for of the other things that are in an orator each man claims for himself some part, but the greatest power of speaking—that is, of "eloquing"—is granted to this man alone.

For although certain philosophers too have spoken ornately—since Theophrastus took his name from the divinity of his speech, and Aristotle challenged Isocrates himself, and they say that the Muses spoke, as it were, with the voice of Xenophon, and far above all who have ever written or spoken Plato stood out as prince both in sweetness and in weight—yet the speech of these men has neither the sinews nor the stings of the orator and of the forum.

They speak with the learned, whose minds they prefer to soothe rather than to incite, and they speak of matters peaceful and least turbulent, for the sake of teaching, not of capturing; so that, in this very thing, that they hunt after some delight in their speaking, they seem to some to do more than is necessary. From this kind, therefore, it is not difficult to set apart that eloquence of which we now treat.

For the speech of the philosophers is soft and, as it were, born in the shade, furnished neither with popular thoughts nor with popular words, nor bound by rhythms, but loosed more freely; it has nothing wrathful, nothing envious, nothing fierce, nothing pitiful, nothing crafty—chaste, modest, in a certain way an uncorrupted maiden. And so it is called conversation rather than oratory. For although all speech is "oration," yet the speech of the orator alone is marked with this proper name.

The resemblance of the sophists, of whom I spoke above, seems to need to be more sharply distinguished, for they all wish to pursue the same flowers that the orator employs in his cases. But in this they differ: that, since it is their aim not to disturb minds but rather to soothe them, and not so much to persuade as to delight, they both do this more openly than we and more frequently, and they seek out neat thoughts rather than plausible ones, often depart from the matter, weave in fables, transfer words from a higher source and arrange them as painters arrange a variety of colours, match equals with equals, set opposites against contraries, and very often end their clauses alike.

To this kind history is the near neighbour, in which both narration is done ornately and often a region or a battle is described; harangues, too, and exhortations are inserted; but in these something drawn-out and flowing is sought, not this twisted and keen oratory. From these, not much otherwise than from the poets, this eloquence which we seek must be called apart. For the poets, too, have raised a question, what that thing might be by which they themselves differed from the orators: formerly they seemed to differ most in rhythm and verse, but now among the orators rhythm itself has grown common.

For whatever it is that falls under some measure of the ears, even if it be without verse—for that indeed is a fault of oratory—is called number, which in Greek is called rhythmos. And so I see that it has seemed to some that the diction of Plato and of Democritus, though it stand apart from verse, yet, because it is borne along more impetuously and uses the brightest lights of words, is rather to be deemed a poem than the diction of the comic poets; in whom, save that there are little verses, there is nothing else unlike everyday talk. Yet that is not the greatest thing about the poet, though he is the more praiseworthy in this, that he pursues the virtues of the orator, while being bound the more tightly by verse.

But for my part, although the voice of certain poets is grand and ornate, yet, as I judge that in it there is a greater licence than in us for making and joining words, so I observe too that not a few of them serve their pleasure by words rather than by matter; nor indeed, if there is one thing alike among them—and that is the judgment and choice of words—can the unlikeness in other matters on that account not be perceived; but that is neither doubtful, and, if it has any matter for inquiry, this very thing is nonetheless not necessary to what we have proposed. The orator, therefore, set apart from the eloquence of the philosophers, of the sophists, of the historians, of the poets, must be unfolded by us, what sort of man he is to be.

He will be eloquent, then—for this is the man we seek on the authority of Antonius—he who in the forum and in civil cases will so speak as to prove, to delight, to bend. To prove belongs to necessity, to delight to sweetness, to bend to victory: for this alone of all things can do most toward winning cases. But as many as are the offices of the orator, so many are the kinds of speaking: subtle in proving, moderate in delighting, vehement in bending; in which one thing lies all the power of the orator.

Of great judgment, therefore, and of the highest faculty too will that governor and, as it were, temperer of this threefold variety have to be; for he will both judge what is needful in each case and will be able to speak in whatever way the case shall demand. But the foundation of eloquence, as of all else, is wisdom. For as in life, so in oratory, nothing is more difficult than to see what is becoming. The Greeks call this prepon; let us, for our part, call it "the becoming." Concerning it many fine precepts are given, and the matter is most worthy of knowledge; through ignorance of it men err not only in life but very often both in poems and in oratory.

Now what is becoming the orator must see not in his thoughts alone but also in his words. For not every fortune, not every rank, not every authority, not every age, nor indeed every place or time or hearer is to be handled with the same kind of words or of thoughts; and always, in every part of oratory as of life, what is becoming must be considered; which depends both on the matter in hand and on the persons both of those who speak and of those who hear.

And so this topic, which lies far and wide open, the philosophers are wont to treat in their works on duties—not when they dispute of the right itself, for that indeed is one thing—the grammarians in the poets, the eloquent in every kind and part of cases. For how unbecoming it is, when you speak before a single judge about gutter-drippings, to use the amplest words and commonplaces; and to speak of the majesty of the Roman people in a subdued and plain manner! Here men err in the whole kind; but in the person men err either in their own, or in that of the judges, or even of their adversaries, and not in the matter only but often in the word; though without matter no word has any force, yet the same matter is often either approved or rejected when set forth in one word or another.

And in all things one must see how far; for though each thing has its own measure, yet too much offends more than too little; in which Apelles said that those painters too erred who did not perceive what was enough. This is a great topic, Brutus—as you are well aware—and demands another great volume; but for the matter in hand this is enough. When we say "this is becoming"—which we constantly use of all things said and done, the least and the greatest—when, I say, we say "this is becoming," "that is not becoming," and it appears everywhere how great a thing it is, and it is placed in one matter while it is wholly another thing whether you say "becoming" or "fitting";—for "fitting" declares the perfection of a duty,

which both must always be used and by all, while "becoming" means, as it were, what is apt and consonant with the time and the person; and this holds good very often in deeds, and likewise in words, and finally in countenance and gesture and gait; and so, on the other hand, the "unbecoming." And if the poet shuns this as the greatest fault—who errs even when he attaches the speech of a good man to a bad one, or of a wise man to a fool; if, finally, that painter saw, when in the sacrifice of Iphigenia Calchas was sad, Ulysses sadder, Menelaus mourning, that the head of Agamemnon must be veiled, since he could not imitate that supreme grief with his brush; if, finally, the actor asks what is becoming—what are we to think the orator must do? But since this is so great a thing, what the orator is to do in cases and in their, as it were, members, he himself will see: this at least is clear, that not only the parts of an oration but whole cases too must be handled, some in one form of speaking, others in another.

It follows that for each kind the mark and formula must be sought: a great and arduous work, as we have already often said; but at the outset we had to consider what we were doing, while now, wherever we are borne, the sails must surely be spread. And first there must be fashioned by us that man whom alone they call Attic.

He is subdued and lowly, imitating ordinary usage, differing from the unskilled more in fact than in seeming. And so those who hear him, however inarticulate they themselves may be, nevertheless trust that they can speak in that manner. For the plainness of his oratory does indeed seem imitable to one who reckons it, but nothing is less so to one who tries. For though it is not of the fullest blood, it ought nevertheless to have some sap, so that, even if it lack those greatest strengths, it may be, so to speak, of sound health.

First, then, let us free him, as it were, from the bonds of rhythms. For there are certain oratorical rhythms, as you know, which we shall treat of soon, to be observed by a certain method, but in another kind of oratory; in this one they are wholly to be left aside. Let there be something loosed, yet not wandering, so that he may seem to walk freely, not to stray licentiously. Let him neglect even to cement word to word, as it were. For that very thing—the hiatus and clashing of vowels—has a certain softness, and something that betokens a not ungraceful carelessness in one who labours over the matter rather than over the words.

But concerning the rest there will need to be care, when these two things have been made freer for him: the periodic round and the gluing-together of words. For those very contracted and minute matters are not to be handled carelessly, but there is even a careful kind of carelessness. For as some women are said to be unadorned, as if that very thing became them, so this subtle oratory delights even when uncombed; for there is in each something whereby it is the more charming, but so as not to be apparent. Then will all conspicuous ornament, like that of pearls, be removed;

not even the curling-irons will be applied; and all the cosmetics of a feigned whiteness and ruddiness will be repelled; only elegance and neatness will remain. The speech will be pure and Latin; it will be spoken clearly and plainly; what is becoming will be looked to all around; one thing will be absent—what Theophrastus reckons fourth among the praises of oratory: that ornament, sweet and overflowing. Keen and frequent thoughts will be set down, and dug out, I know not whence, from the hidden depths; and—what will reign in this orator—there will be a modest use of the orator's, as it were, furniture.

For we have, in a manner, our own furniture, which lies in adornments—one of matters, the other of words. Now the adornment of words is twofold: one of single words, the other of words arranged together. The single word is approved in proper and customary words, because it either sounds best or makes the matter clearest; in unfamiliar words it is either a thing transferred and made from elsewhere as if on loan, or a thing made by the man himself and new, or one ancient and unaccustomed; but even unaccustomed and ancient words belong among the proper, except that we use them rarely.

Arranged words have adornment if they produce some trimness which would not remain, though the thought remains, if the words were changed; for the adornments of thoughts which remain even if you change the words are indeed very many, but those that stand out are fewer.

Therefore that plain orator, provided he is elegant, will be neither bold in coining words, but modest and sparing in transferring them, and rather lowly in the ancient ones and in the rest of the adornments both of words and of thoughts; in that transference perhaps more frequent, which all talk uses most often, not only of townsmen but even of countrymen: since it is theirs to say that the vines "gem," that the fields "thirst," that the crops are "joyful," that the corn is "luxuriant."

None of these is too boldly said, but it is either like that from which you transfer, or, if a thing has no name of its own, the word seems taken for the sake of teaching, not of play. This adornment this subdued speaker will use a little more freely than the rest, yet not so licentiously as if he were using the amplest kind of speaking; and so that unbecoming thing—which must be understood from what is becoming—appears here too, when some word is transferred from a higher source and that is set in a lowly oration which would have been becoming in another.

But that trimness which lights up the arrangement of words with those lights which the Greeks call schemata, as if certain gestures of oratory—the same word being transferred by them also to the adornments of thoughts—this man indeed, the subtle one, whom certain people rightly call Attic, save only that they call him so and nothing else, applies, but a little more sparingly; for, as in the furnishing of a banquet, withdrawing from magnificence he will wish to seem not only sparing but also elegant, and he will choose what he shall use.

For most things are suited to the very thrift of this orator of whom I speak. For those things of which I spoke before are to be shunned by this keen speaker: equals matched with equals, clauses ending alike and falling in the same fashion, and charms sought, as it were, by the change of a letter—lest a laboured trimness and a certain hunting after delight should appear, manifestly caught in the act;

and likewise, if any repetitions of words call for some straining and outcry, they will be foreign to this subdued kind of oratory; the rest he will be able to use indifferently, only let him loosen and divide the run of words, and use the most customary words and the softest transferences; he will take up also those lights of thoughts which will not be vehemently brilliant. He will not make the commonwealth speak, nor will he call up the dead from the lower world, nor will he, heaping up many things together, bind them in one comprehension. These belong to stronger lungs, and are neither to be expected nor demanded of the man we are fashioning; for he will be more restrained in oratory, as in voice.

But most of those things will suit this plainness too, though he will use the same adornments more roughly; for such is the man we bring in. There will be added a delivery not tragic nor of the stage, but with a moderate movement of the body, yet accomplishing much with the countenance—not that by which they are said to "make faces," but that by which men frankly signify with what feeling they pronounce each thing.

To this kind of oratory will be sprinkled also salty wit, which has wonderful power in speaking; of which there are two kinds, one of pleasantry, the other of raillery. He will use both; the one in narrating something charmingly, the other in throwing and shooting a jest, of which there are several kinds; but now we are doing another thing.

This, however, we do warn: that the orator will so use the laughable that it be neither too frequent, lest it be buffoonish, nor somewhat obscene, lest it be like the mime, nor petulant, lest it be wicked, nor aimed at calamity, lest it be inhuman, nor at crime, lest laughter take the place of hatred; and that it be foreign neither to his own person nor to that of the judges nor to the time. For these things are referred to that "unbecoming."

He will avoid, too, jokes sought-out and not framed on the spur of the moment, but brought from home, which for the most part are frigid. He will spare both friendships and high stations, will avoid incurable insults, will only prick his adversaries, and these too not always nor all of them nor in every way. These things excepted, he will so use salt and pleasantry that, of those new Attic speakers, I have come to know no such man, although that surely is most of all Attic.

This I judge to be the form of the subdued orator, but one great nonetheless and a genuine and true-born Attic; since whatever is salty or wholesome in oratory is the property of the Attic writers. Of these, however, not all are witty: Lysias well enough, and Hyperides; Demades is reported beyond the rest; Demosthenes is held to have less of it—though to me nothing seems more urbane, but he was not so much given to raillery as to pleasantry; and that is the mark of a keener genius, this of a greater art.

There is another kind richer and somewhat more robust than this lowly one of which we have spoken, but more subdued than that amplest one of which we shall now speak. In this kind there is the very least of sinew, but the very most of sweetness. For it is fuller than this finely-wrought one, but more subdued than that ornate and copious one.

To this all the adornments of speaking are suited, and there is the most of sweetness in this form of oratory. In it many flourished among the Greeks, but Demetrius of Phalerum, in my judgment, surpassed the rest; whose oratory, while it flows calmly and quietly, is lit up, as it were, by certain stars—words transferred and changed. By "transferred" I mean, as I have often said already, those that are carried over from another thing by way of likeness, for the sake either of sweetness or of poverty; by "changed," those in which, in place of the proper word, another is substituted that means the same, taken from some related thing.

And although this is done by transferring, yet Ennius transferred in one way when he said "Of citadel and of city I am bereft," in another when he said "Bristling Africa trembles with terrible tumult": this the rhetoricians call hypallage, because words are as it were exchanged for words; the grammarians call it metonymy,

because nouns are transferred; Aristotle, moreover, subjoins both these very things to transference, and also abuse, which he calls catachresis, as when we say a "minute" mind for a "small" one; and we abuse neighbouring words, if need be, either because it delights or because it is becoming. Now when several transferences have flowed on continuously, the oratory becomes plainly of another kind; and so the Greeks call this kind allegory—rightly by name, but better in genus is he who calls all those things transferences. These Demetrius of Phalerum most frequents, and they are most sweet; and although transference is abundant in him, yet nowhere are the "changes" more frequent.

Into this same kind of oratory—for I speak of that moderate and tempered one—fall all the lights of words, many also of thoughts; broad and learned disputations will be unfolded by this same man, and commonplaces spoken without contention. Why say more? From the schools of the philosophers such men for the most part come forth; and unless that stronger speaker be set beside him for comparison, this one of whom I speak will of himself win approval.

For there is also a certain notable and flowering kind of oratory, painted and polished, in which all the charms of words, all of thoughts, are entwined. This whole kind has flowed down from the springs of the sophists into the forum; but, scorned by the plain and repulsed by the weighty, it has settled in that middle station of which I speak.

The third is that ample, copious, weighty, ornate kind, in which assuredly is the greatest power. This it is whose ornament and abundance of speaking the nations admired and suffered eloquence to have the greatest weight in their states—but this eloquence which is borne along with a great course and din, which all looked up to, which they admired, which they distrusted their power to attain. To this eloquence it belongs to handle minds, to move them in every way. It now breaks through, now creeps into the feelings; it implants new opinions, it tears up rooted ones.

But there is a great difference between this kind of speaking and the former. He who has laboured in that subtle and keen kind, so as to speak shrewdly and cleverly, and has aimed at nothing higher, is, with this one thing perfected, a great orator, and, if not the greatest, yet he will move least on slippery ground, and, if he once takes his stand, he will never fall. That middle speaker, however, whom I call moderate and tempered, provided only he has sufficiently equipped himself in his own kind, will not dread the doubtful and uncertain chances of speaking; even if at some time he succeeds less well, as often happens, he will yet enter into no great danger: for he cannot fall from a height.

But this speaker of ours, whom we set first—weighty, keen, ardent—if he was born for this one thing alone, or has exercised himself in this alone, or has devoted himself to this one kind, and has not tempered his abundance with those other two kinds, is most of all to be despised. For that subdued speaker, because he speaks shrewdly and with veteran cunning, is already accounted wise; the middle one is sweet; but this most copious one, if he is nothing else, commonly seems scarcely sane enough. For one who can say nothing tranquilly, nothing gently, nothing in a divided, defined, distinct, witty way—especially since cases must be handled partly wholly in that manner, partly in some part—if he begins to inflame the matter when ears are not prepared, he seems to rave among the sane and, like a drunken man, to play the Bacchant among the sober.

We hold him, then, Brutus, the man we seek—but in the mind; for if I had grasped him with my hand, not even he himself, with all his great eloquence, would have persuaded me to let him go. But that eloquent man whom Antonius never saw has surely been found. Who, then, is he? I shall embrace it briefly, and discourse upon it at more length. He is the eloquent man who can speak lowly matters subtly, lofty matters weightily, and middling matters with temperance. No such man, you will say, ever existed.

So be it, granted there was none. For I am disputing what I desire, not what I have seen, and I come back to that form and appearance of the thing, of which I had spoken, drawn from Plato, which, though we do not discern it, we can nevertheless hold in the mind. For I do not seek the eloquent man, nor anything mortal and perishable, but that very thing, possessed of which a man is eloquent; which is nothing else than eloquence itself, which we can see with no eyes but those of the mind. He, then, will be eloquent—to repeat that same thing once more—who shall be able to speak small things subduedly, middling things temperately, great things weightily.

My whole case for Caecina turned on the words of an interdict: we unfolded entangled matters by defining, we praised the civil law, we distinguished ambiguous words. In the Manilian law Pompey had to be adorned: with tempered oratory we pursued the abundance of adorning. The whole right of preserving the majesty of the state was contained in the case of Rabirius: therefore in it we blazed forth in every kind of amplification.

But these things must at times be tempered and varied. What kind, then, is not found in the seven books of the accusation? what in the case of Habitus? what in that of Cornelius? what in very many of our defences? which examples I would have selected, had I not thought them either well known, or that those who sought them could read them for themselves. For there is no praise in any kind whatever of which there is not in our orations some specimen, if not a perfection, yet at least an attempt and a sketch.

We do not attain it; yet we see what it is becoming to pursue. For we are not now speaking of ourselves, but of the matter; in which we are so far from admiring our own work, and are so hard to please and so peevish, that not even Demosthenes himself satisfies us; who, although he stands out alone above all in every kind of speaking, yet does not always fill my ears; so greedy and capacious are they, and often they desire something immeasurable and infinite.

But nevertheless, since you have come to know this orator most diligently and wholly, together with that most zealous student of him, Pammenes, when you were at Athens, and do not let him out of your hands, and yet read our works too—you surely see that he accomplishes much, that we attempt much; that he is able, that we wish, to speak in whatever way the case demands. For he, being great, both came after great men himself and had the greatest orators as his contemporaries; we have had less. We should have done a great thing, if indeed we had been able to reach what we strive for, in that city in which, as Antonius says, no eloquent man had ever been heard.

And yet, if Crassus did not seem eloquent to Antonius, or to himself, never would Cotta have seemed so, never Sulpicius, never Hortensius; for Cotta spoke nothing amply, Sulpicius nothing gently, Hortensius not many things weightily; the earlier men, Crassus I mean and Antonius, were more apt for every kind. We have found, then, that the ears of the state were starved of this manifold oratory, evenly poured forth into all the kinds; and we were the first—whoever we were, and however little we spoke—to turn them to incredible eagerness for hearing this kind.

With what great applause did we, as very young men, deliver those passages which we afterward began to feel, somewhat later, had by no means cooled enough: "For what is so common as breath to the living, earth to the dead, the sea to those tossed by it, the shore to the shipwrecked? They so live, while they can, that they cannot draw breath from heaven; they so die that their bones do not touch the earth; they are so tossed by the waves that they are never washed clean; they are at last so cast forth that not even dead do they find rest among the rocks"—and what follows; for all these are such as are praised in a young man not so much for substance and ripeness as for hope and expectation. From this same talent come those riper things: "wife of the son-in-law, stepmother of the son, rival of the daughter."

Nor indeed was there in us this one ardour alone, to say everything in this manner. For that very youthful redundance has many things subdued, some even a little more cheerful, as in the cases for Habitus, for Cornelius, and several others. For no orator wrote so many things even in Greek leisure as are our writings, and these have that very variety which I approve.

Or should I grant to Homer, to Ennius, to the rest of the poets, and most of all to the tragic, that they should not in all places use the same straining, and should often change it, and sometimes even come near to the everyday kind of talk—and should I myself never depart from that fiercest straining? But why do I bring forward the poets, of divine genius? We have seen actors than whom nothing could be more excellent in their kind, who not only gave satisfaction in the most dissimilar parts, while yet they kept within their own kind, but whom we have seen greatly please both as comedians in tragedies and as tragedians in comedies: shall I not labour?

When I say "I," Brutus, I mean you; for in me, indeed, what was to be has long ago been wrought; but will you conduct all cases in the same manner? or will you reject some kind of case? or in the same cases will you keep one and the same breath without any change? Demosthenes indeed—whose likeness in bronze I lately saw among the images of yourself and your kin, when I had come to you at your Tusculan villa, because I believe you love him—yields nothing to Lysias in subtlety, nothing to Hyperides in cleverness and keenness, nothing to Aeschines in smoothness and splendour of words.

Many whole orations of his are subtle, as that against Leptines; many wholly weighty, as certain of the Philippics; many varied, as that against Aeschines about the false embassy, and as that against the same on behalf of the cause of Ctesiphon. Then, as often as he wishes, he seizes that middle kind, and, departing from the weightiest, glides into it by preference. Yet he stirs applause, and accomplishes most in speaking, just when he uses the passages of weight.

But let us go away from this man for a little, since indeed we are inquiring about the kind, not about the man: let us rather unfold the power and nature of the thing itself, that is, of eloquence. Let us, however, remember what we have already said before, that we shall say nothing for the sake of precept, and shall rather so act as to seem to speak as appraisers, not as masters. In this, however, we often go further, because we see that not only you will read these things—you who have them far better known than we, who seem, as it were, to teach—but that this book, even if less by our recommendation, must yet by your name be published abroad.

I think, then, that it belongs to the perfectly eloquent man not only to have that faculty which is his own, of speaking diffusely and broadly, but also to take up the neighbouring and bordering science of the dialecticians. Although speech seems to be one thing, disputation another, and to "talk" not the same as to "speak," yet both lie in discoursing: let the method of disputing and of talking belong to the dialecticians, but that of speaking and adorning to the orators. Zeno, indeed, from whom comes the school of the Stoics, was wont to demonstrate with his hand what difference there was between these arts; for when he had pressed his fingers together and made a fist, he said dialectic was of that sort; but when he had drawn them apart and spread out his hand, he said eloquence was like that open palm.

And even before him Aristotle, at the beginning of his Art of Rhetoric, says that that art corresponds, as it were, from the other side, to dialectic, so that they differ between themselves in this, evidently—that this method of speaking is broader, that of talking more contracted. I wish, therefore, that to this supreme man every method of talking which can be drawn toward speaking be known; which matter—as does not in the least escape you, who are versed in these arts—has had a twofold way of teaching. For Aristotle himself handed down very many precepts of discoursing, and afterward those who are called dialecticians brought forth many thornier ones.

For my part, I judge that he who is led by the praise of eloquence should not be wholly raw in these matters, but instructed either in that ancient discipline or in this of Chrysippus. Let him first know the force, the nature, the kinds of words, both single and coupled; then in how many ways each thing is said; by what method it is judged whether a thing is true or false; what follows from each, what is consequent to each, or contrary; and, since many things are said ambiguously, in what manner each of them ought to be divided and explained. These things the orator must hold—for they often occur—but, because of themselves they are somewhat squalid, there will need to be applied in unfolding them a certain brightness of oratory.

And since in all things that are taught by method and rule it must first be established what each thing is—for unless it is agreed among those who debate what that thing is which is in dispute, neither can the matter ever be rightly discussed nor brought to an end—our mind must often be unfolded in words concerning each matter, and the wrapped-up notion of a thing must be opened by defining, since indeed a definition is a statement which shows, as briefly as may be, what the thing in question is; then, as you know, when the genus of each thing has been unfolded, it must be seen what are the forms or parts of that genus, so that the whole discourse may be distributed into them.

There will be, therefore, this faculty in the man whom we wish to be eloquent, that he can define a thing—and not do it so compressedly and narrowly as is usual in those most learned disputations, but both more plainly and also more richly and more suited to common judgment and popular intelligence; and likewise, when the matter shall require, he will distribute and divide a universal genus into fixed species, so that none is either passed over or redundant. But when he is to do this, or in what manner, nothing for the present, since, as I said above, I wish to be a judge, not a teacher.

Nor indeed let him be equipped by the dialecticians alone, and have all the topics of philosophy known and handled. For nothing about religion, nothing about death, nothing about piety, nothing about love of country, nothing about good things or bad, nothing about virtues or vices, nothing about duty, nothing about pain, nothing about pleasure, nothing about the disturbances and errors of the mind—which often fall into cases and are handled too meagrely—nothing, I say, can be said and unfolded weightily, amply, copiously without that knowledge of which I have spoken.

I am speaking, even now, of the matter of oratory, not of the kind of speaking itself. For I wish the orator first to have a matter to speak of, worthy of learned ears, before he considers in what words he is to say each thing; whom too—that he may be the grander and, in a certain way, the more lofty, as I said above of Pericles—I would not have ignorant even of the natural philosophers. Assuredly in all things, when he returns from heavenly matters to human, he will both speak and feel more loftily and magnificently.

When he has come to know those divine things, I would not have him ignorant of these human ones either. Let him hold the civil law, which forensic cases daily need. For what is baser than to undertake the patronage of legal and civil controversies, when you are ignorant of the laws and of the civil law? Let him learn also the order of things done and of ancient memory—most of all, of course, that of our own state, but also of imperious peoples and illustrious kings; which labour our friend Atticus lightened for us, who, having preserved and marked the dates, while he passed over nothing illustrious, bound up the memory of seven hundred years in a single book. But to be ignorant of what happened before you were born—that is to be always a child. For what is the life of a man, unless it is woven together by the memory of ancient things with the age of those who went before? And the recalling of antiquity, and the bringing-forward of examples, brings to oratory, with the greatest delight, both authority and credit.

Thus equipped, then, he will come to cases, of which he will have first known the very kinds. For it will be clear to him that nothing can be in dispute in which either the matter or the words do not make the controversy: the matter, either of the true, or of the right, or of the name; the words, either of the ambiguous or of the contrary. For if at any time one thing seems to be in the meaning, another in the words, there is a certain kind of ambiguity which is wont to arise from an omitted word, in which we see two things signified—that which is proper to ambiguities.

Since the kinds of cases are so few, the precepts of arguments too are few. There have been handed down twofold topics from which they are drawn: some from the things themselves, others borrowed. The handling of the matters, then, makes an oration admirable; for the matters themselves lie in very easy knowing. For what now follows that belongs to art, except to begin the oration in such a way that the hearer is either won over, or roused, or made ready to learn; to set forth the matter briefly and plausibly and clearly, so that what is being done can be understood; to confirm one's own points, to overthrow the adversary's, and to do this not confusedly but by concluding the several arguments in such a way that there is brought about what is consequent to those things which are assumed for the confirming of each point; and after all, in the peroration, to conclude by inflaming or quenching? How he is to handle these parts severally is hard to say in this place; for they are not always handled in one way.

But since I am seeking not whom I should teach but whom I should approve, I shall first approve the man who has seen what is becoming. For this wisdom must most of all be applied by the eloquent man, that he be the governor of times and persons. For I think one must speak neither always, nor before all, nor against all, nor for all, nor with all in the same manner. He, then, will be eloquent who can fit his oratory to whatever shall be becoming. And when he has determined this, then, as each thing is to be said, so he will say it, neither plain things meagrely nor grand things minutely, nor again the contrary, but his oratory will be even and equal to the matters themselves.

The openings modest, not yet kindled with lofty words, but keen in their thoughts, either for the offence of the adversary or for the commendation of himself. The narratives credible, and unfolded clearly not in the historical but almost in everyday speech. Then, if the case is slight, then there will be a slight thread of arguing too, both in teaching and in refuting, and this will be so held that as great an accession is made to the oratory as to the matter.

But when there falls out a case in which the power of eloquence can be brought forth, then the orator will pour himself forth more broadly, then he will rule and bend men's minds and so affect them as he wills—that is, as the nature of the case and the reason of the time shall demand. But all that admirable ornament of his, on account of which eloquence rose into so great honour, will be twofold. For while every part of the oration ought to be praiseworthy, so that no word falls from him but is either weighty or elegant, yet there are two parts that are most luminous and, as it were, full of action: one of which I place in the question of the universal kind, which, as I said above, the Greeks call thesis; the other in the heightening and amplifying of matters, which is by the same men named auxesis.

Which, though it ought to be evenly diffused throughout the whole body of the oration, will yet most excel in the commonplaces; which are called "common" for this reason, that they seem to be the same for many cases, but they will have to be made proper to single ones. But that part of the oration which concerns the universal kind often contains whole cases. For whatever it is in which there is, as it were, the contest of the controversy, which in Greek is called the krinomenon, that, it is held, should be so spoken of that it is led over to the perpetual question, and the discourse is made about the universal kind—except when the dispute is about the true, which is wont to be inquired into by conjecture.

And it will be said not in the manner of the Peripatetics—for theirs is an elegant exercise, established ever since Aristotle—but somewhat more sinewy, and matters of general kind will be so spoken of that on behalf of the accused many things are said gently, and against the adversaries harshly. But for heightening matters, and on the other side for casting them down, there is nothing that oratory cannot accomplish; which must be done amid the very arguments, as often as there is given a place either for amplifying or for diminishing, and almost without limit in the peroration.

For two things remain which, well handled by the orator, make eloquence admirable. Of these one is what the Greeks call ethikon, suited to characters and to manners and to all the custom of life; the other is what the same men name pathetikon, by which minds are disturbed and stirred, and in which alone oratory reigns. The former is courteous, pleasant, prepared for winning goodwill; this latter is vehement, kindled, urged on, by which cases are snatched away: which, when it is borne along impetuously, can be withstood by no means whatever.

By which kind we, of middling power or even far less, but always using a great onset, have often cast our adversaries from their whole standing. To us, on behalf of an intimate defendant, the supreme orator Hortensius made no answer; by us the most audacious of men, Catiline, accused in the senate, was struck dumb; to us, when in a private case, great and weighty, the elder Curio had begun to answer, he suddenly sat down, saying that his memory had been snatched from him by poisons.

What shall I say of appeals to pity? Of which I have made the more use because, even if we spoke as several advocates, they nonetheless all left the peroration to me; in which, that I might seem to excel, I attained it not by genius but by grief. These qualities, whatever they may be in me—and it grieves me how great they are—yet appear in the orations, although the books lack that breath on account of which those same things, when they are pleaded, are wont to seem greater than when they are read.

Nor indeed is the mind of the judges to be moved by pity alone—which we are wont to use so feelingly that, while concluding, we have held an infant child in our arms; that in another case, having roused a noble defendant and lifted up his little son too, we have filled the forum with wailing and lamentation—but it must also be brought about that the judge grow angry and be appeased, that he envy and favour, that he despise and admire, that he hate and love, that he desire and disdain, that he hope and fear, that he be glad and grieve; in which variety the accusation will furnish examples of the harsher passions, my defences of the gentler.

For in no manner can the mind of the hearer be either roused or soothed by a measure not attempted by me—I would say "perfected," if I judged it so, and if in truth I did not dread the charge of arrogance; but, as I said above, no force of genius, but a great force of feeling kindles me, so that I cannot hold myself; nor would the man who heard ever be kindled, unless the oratory came to him burning. I would use examples of my own household, had you not read them; I would use those of others, either Latin, if I could find any, or Greek, if it were becoming. But of Crassus there are very few, and these not of judicial cases; nothing of Antonius, nothing of Cotta, nothing of Sulpicius; Hortensius spoke better than he wrote.

But of this power which we seek let us conjecture how great it is, since we have no example—or, if we follow examples, let us take them from Demosthenes, and that from continuous discourse, from that passage in the trial of Ctesiphon where he set about speaking of his own deeds, counsels, and services to the state. That oration, assuredly, can be so enclosed within the form which is implanted in our minds that no greater eloquence is even required.

But now the form remains, and that "character," as it is called; what sort it ought to be can be understood from what has been said above. For we have touched on the lights both of single words and of arranged ones; in which he will so abound that no word goes forth from his mouth but is either elegant or weighty; and from every kind the transferences will be most frequent, because these, on account of their likeness, carry men's minds across and bring them back and move them this way and that—which motion of thought, swiftly stirred, of itself delights. And the rest that are taken from the arrangement of words, as it were lights, bring great ornament to the oration; for they are like those things which, in the ample adornment of the stage or the forum, are called insignia—not because they alone adorn, but because they stand out.
